The experimental scope is substantial: two architecture families, sizes from 0.5B to 4B, 20- and 140-token-per-parameter regimes, broad weight-decay sweeps for several configurations, six fine-tuning datasets, and multiple generation-based evaluation metrics.

The overtrained OLMo result is especially informative: weight decay 0.3 produces slightly worse pretraining loss than 0.1 but noticeably better post-fine-tuning performance, directly demonstrating that pretraining loss need not determine the best downstream checkpoint.

The representation, attention pseudo-rank, and train-validation-gap analyses provide several plausible hypotheses for future mechanistic work rather than reporting only an empirical hyperparameter sweep.

The paper is generally well organized, visually polished, and unusually candid about unstable loss-performance correlations, possible changes beyond 140 TPP, and limited extrapolation to larger or more heavily overtrained models.
weaknesses: Soundness: the operational definition of plasticity is inadequate for the central causal claim. Final fine-tuned accuracy combines a checkpoint's initial task capability, representation quality, and amount learned during fine-tuning. The paper does not report pre/post improvement, learning curves, performance conditioned on matched starting capability, or learning of controlled novel information. Consequently, the experiments support that weight decay changes transfer performance, but not cleanly that it increases plasticity or the ability to learn new knowledge.

Soundness: no repeated pretraining or fine-tuning runs, uncertainty intervals, or statistical tests are reported. Several claimed improvements are small, while stochastic variation at this scale may be material. Fixed fine-tuning hyperparameters and three epochs may also favor some pretrained variants; robustness to fine-tuning learning rate, training budget, and seed is not established.

The strongest optimality and generality language exceeds the evidence. Llama-2-4B is tested at only two decay values and OLMo-2-1B-140x at three, so their reported optima are merely the best sampled points. Only one architecture/configuration is evaluated at 140 TPP, and all models are at most 4B, limiting conclusions about modern large or heavily overtrained LLMs.

The six tasks do not provide six independent evaluation sets: MetaMathQA and SimpleScaling are both evaluated on the same GSM8KPlatinum plus MATH questions. The reported all-task value uses 23,102 examples—the sum of dataset sizes—so it appears to be example-weighted and counts this shared math test set twice rather than macro-averaging tasks. This can materially bias the headline aggregate trends.

The mechanistic claims are correlational and substantially overstated. Better linear-probe accuracy does not show that linear separability mediates fine-tuning gains; the high pooled probe/downstream correlation is confounded by architecture and scale, while several within-configuration correlations are weak or negative. Low attention rank largely reproduces prior work and is not causally connected to plasticity, and the tiny train-validation-gap analysis covers only OLMo-2-1B at 20 TPP.

The correlation analysis has too few points for reliable inference—most notably, the 4B series has two observations, making correlations of ±1 automatic. Leave-one-out instability highlights this weakness but does not itself strengthen the claimed relationship. Effect sizes with uncertainty and appropriately powered comparisons are needed.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful architecture and optimizer tables. The manuscript does not provide code or checkpoint links, repository commits, random seeds, exact validation-set construction, cleaning rules, answer-extraction procedures, or sufficient linear-probe training details. Reproducing the full study would also require very substantial compute.

Limitations and ethics are only partially treated. Scale and training-duration limitations are acknowledged, but the paper does not discuss dataset licensing or contamination, the reliability and possible biases of the Skywork reward-model evaluator, medical-domain misuse, or the environmental cost of the extensive pretraining sweep. These are not necessarily fatal ethical issues, but they should be documented. Presentation also suffers from dense appendix figures and several copyediting errors.

strengths: The paper asks a practically important and underexplored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters should be selected for downstream adaptability rather than validation loss alone. The observed reversal for OLMo-2-1B at 140 TPP—where weight decay 0.3/1.0 worsens pretraining loss relative to 0.1 but improves post-fine-tuning performance—is particularly informative.

The experimental scope is substantial: five configurations spanning Llama-2 and OLMo-2 architectures, 0.5B–4B parameters, 20 and 140 tokens per parameter, six fine-tuning datasets, and several decoding/evaluation metrics. The appendix reports core architecture, pretraining, and fine-tuning hyperparameters.

The main qualitative trend—moderately stronger pretraining weight decay often improves performance after fixed-budget fine-tuning—appears across multiple configurations. The degradation at extremely large decay values also usefully demonstrates that the effect is not unbounded.

The representation, attention-rank, and train–validation-gap analyses offer several plausible hypotheses for future mechanistic study. The paper is generally readable, visually polished, and appropriately describes some of these explanations as conjectures.
The work appears low-risk from a research-ethics perspective, and the medical benchmark is used for model evaluation rather than clinical deployment.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central evidence appears to use only one pretraining and one fine-tuning run per condition. No seeds, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or uncertainty from stochastic decoding are reported. Several gains are small, and the leave-one-out analysis itself shows unstable correlations. Consequently, it is unclear which differences are reproducible rather than run-to-run variation.

The operational definition of plasticity is too confounded to support the stronger claim that weight decay improves an intrinsic capacity to learn. Final accuracy after three fixed fine-tuning epochs also depends on pretrained knowledge, representation quality, weight scale, optimization speed, and interactions with the single chosen fine-tuning learning rate. Learning curves, matched starting-capability controls, fine-tuning hyperparameter sweeps, or direct measures of parameter/representation change are absent.

The downstream datasets do not cleanly test acquisition of genuinely new knowledge: several are common public corpora that may overlap conceptually or literally with web pretraining data. The study therefore establishes an association with post-SFT performance more convincingly than it establishes improved learning of new information.

The paper overstates consistency. Appendix Figure 7 contains non-monotonic or worsening results for some task–metric–model combinations, while the headline aggregate appears to pool 23,102 examples, heavily weighting the larger RACE and math test sets rather than giving each of the six tasks equal weight. Per-task uncertainty and macro-averaged results are not provided.

The claimed mechanisms are correlational rather than explanatory. Linear-probe accuracy can reflect ordinary pretrained capability, and its pooled correlation with downstream performance is confounded by architecture, scale, and training regime. Lower attention pseudo-rank largely confirms prior work, but no intervention or mediation analysis connects rank to plasticity. The overfitting result is shown only for OLMo-2-1B at 20 TPP, has a very small absolute range, and lacks uncertainty or sufficient details about how training-set loss was re-estimated.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter tables: there is no artifact-release statement, code/checkpoint link, seed information, exact dataset-cleaning procedure, validation-set construction, evaluation prompts and answer extraction, linear-probe training protocol, or full sampling details. These omissions would make exact replication expensive and difficult.

Presentation and limitations treatment are incomplete. Dense appendix plots are difficult to inspect, Equation 1–2 presents the AdamW update in a confusing order, and there is no dedicated limitations or ethics discussion covering contamination, dependence on small-to-mid-scale models, sensitivity to fine-tuning settings, dataset licensing, or the substantial compute required. Overall, the empirical signal is promising and potentially useful, but missing uncertainty and controls prevent reliable support for the paper's central intrinsic-plasticity and mechanistic claims.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled weight-decay sweeps provide substantial evidence for the main empirical observation. Results span two model families, five model/compute configurations up to 4B parameters, six downstream tasks, and several correctness and response-quality metrics.

Soundness: The OLMo-2-1B-140x result is especially informative: weight decay 0.1 has the best pretraining loss, whereas 0.3 and 1.0 yield better post-fine-tuning performance. This directly demonstrates that pretraining-loss-based selection can be suboptimal for downstream use.

Significance: Choosing pretraining hyperparameters for end-to-end performance rather than pretraining loss alone is practically important. The finding could influence expensive model-training decisions even if its optimal numerical setting does not generalize universally.

Originality: The paper connects weight decay during language-model pretraining to subsequent adaptability, an underexplored question. The extensive end-to-end study is novel, while the representation, rank, and overfitting analyses offer useful supporting perspectives.

Presentation: The research question, experimental progression, and principal conclusions are easy to follow. The appendices report architectures, token budgets, weight-decay grids, fine-tuning datasets, sample sizes, and major optimization hyperparameters.

The manuscript appropriately acknowledges that the preferred weight decay may depend on scale, training duration, learning-rate schedule, and objective, and it labels some mechanistic interpretations as conjectures. The experiments pose limited immediate ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: Post-fine-tuning performance alone is an incomplete measure of plasticity. It conflates ability to learn during fine-tuning with pretrained knowledge and representation quality. Initial task performance, learning curves, fine-tuning training loss, or improvement relative to the pretrained baseline would more directly substantiate the central plasticity claim.

The paper reports no repeated pretraining or fine-tuning runs, confidence intervals, or seed-sensitivity analysis. Some differences are modest and several sweeps are sparse—only two weight-decay settings for Llama-2-4B and three for OLMo-2-1B-140x—so claims about optimal values and consistency cannot be separated cleanly from stochastic variation.

Several statements are broader than the evidence. Individual-task curves are not uniformly monotonic, and the paper sometimes describes the effect as consistent across all tasks and metrics. The evidence supports a strong average tendency within the tested settings, not a universal improvement.

The mechanistic section is correlational rather than explanatory. Better probe accuracy does not establish that linear separability causes plasticity; pooled correlations are confounded by model family and scale. Reduced attention rank largely confirms prior work, while the train-validation-gap analysis covers only OLMo-2-1B-20x and has no uncertainty analysis. No intervention or mediation test connects these observations to downstream gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter tables. The manuscript does not provide code or checkpoints, precise data sampling/order and random seeds, complete evaluation prompts and answer-extraction procedures, fine-tuning/probing seed details, or sufficiently detailed linear-probe training specifications. Reproducing the very expensive pretraining study would therefore be difficult.

Presentation would benefit from numerical result tables and uncertainty estimates; many conclusions currently require reading dense multi-panel plots. There are also minor typographical and wording issues.

Limitations and ethics treatment is only partial. Scale and training-duration limits are discussed honestly, but the manuscript does not foreground the missing replication, the limitations of its plasticity operationalization, dataset licensing/privacy considerations, compute costs, or the caution needed when interpreting medical-benchmark performance. These concerns reduce confidence and reach but do not outweigh the paper's useful contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical trend is broad and unusually compute-intensive: weight decay is swept across Llama-2 and OLMo-2, 0.5B–4B parameters, 20 and 140 tokens-per-parameter regimes, six chain-of-thought datasets, five language/commonsense datasets, and safety alignment. The downstream advantage of larger-than-default pretraining weight decay recurs across most settings.

Soundness: The paper goes beyond a single default recipe by jointly varying pretraining learning rate and by sweeping fine-tuning learning rate, weight decay, and batch size. These controls materially strengthen the conclusion that the observed trend is not merely caused by one poorly chosen fine-tuning configuration.

Significance: Demonstrating that the weight decay minimizing pretraining validation loss can differ from the value maximizing post-fine-tuning performance is practically important for end-to-end language-model development and questions a common model-selection assumption.

Originality: The framing of pretraining weight decay as a determinant of later adaptability is fresh, and the paper connects it to representation separability, attention-matrix rank, and train–validation gaps. The attention-rank results also extend prior work to more modern architectures and larger training scales.

Presentation: The manuscript is clear, well organized, and unusually transparent about scope. The appendix provides architectures, token budgets, optimizer settings, downstream dataset sizes, extensive per-task plots, trade-off analyses, and hyperparameter robustness checks.

Limitations and ethics: The authors appropriately acknowledge that their mechanistic evidence is correlational, that some model groups have few configurations, and that conclusions may not extrapolate beyond 4B models, 140 TPP, or supervised fine-tuning. The safety-alignment experiment is relevant, and no unresolved major ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The paper operationalizes plasticity as final downstream performance after fine-tuning, but this does not isolate an ability to adapt. It also reflects the pretrained model’s initial task knowledge and representation quality. The appendix compares upstream benchmark accuracy, but the decisive experiment would report pre-fine-tuning performance, improvement from that baseline, learning curves or sample efficiency, and training-set fitting on each actual downstream task. Consequently, the evidence securely supports improved post-fine-tuning performance, but only indirectly supports the stronger plasticity interpretation.

Soundness and reproducibility: The manuscript reports no repeated pretraining or fine-tuning seeds, uncertainty across runs, or significance tests for the main reasoning and knowledge results. Each weight-decay point appears to be a single expensive training trajectory. Consistency across many tasks is reassuring, but shared checkpoints induce correlated observations, and some claimed differences are small. Calling the effect causal merely because weight decay is the intended changed variable is too strong without demonstrating robustness to stochastic training variation.

Soundness: The three proposed mechanisms are associations induced by the same intervention rather than tests of mediation. Higher linear-probe accuracy may simply indicate better task-relevant representations; lower attention pseudo-rank and a smaller train–validation gap are not shown to cause adaptability. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but phrases such as “mechanistic perspective” and “potential explanation” should remain explicitly conjectural throughout.

Significance/generalization: The largest model is 4B and has only three weight-decay settings; the sole 140-TPP family is approximately 1.5B with four settings. Thus, the recommendation that optimal weight decay exceeds 0.1 is not yet established for contemporary large models, substantially longer training, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, or parameter-efficient adaptation.

Evaluation: The headline chain-of-thought average micro-aggregates examples rather than treating tasks as independent units, and MetaMathQA and SimpleScaling are both evaluated on the same GSM8KPlatinum+MATH test sets. This duplicates evaluation domains and lets larger test sets dominate the aggregate. Macro averages, per-task effect summaries, and hierarchical or paired uncertainty estimates would make the evidence easier to interpret.

Reproducibility: Although datasets, architectures, and many hyperparameters are documented well, important details such as random seeds, number of independent runs, exact checkpoint-selection policy, probe-training configuration, and complete evaluation implementation are absent or unclear. “Models” and “Code” are displayed on the first page, but no accessible artifact information is present in the supplied manuscript. These omissions hinder exact replication of a very expensive study.

Presentation: The main paper sometimes overstates universality, for example saying that higher weight decay “consistently” improves plasticity, despite non-monotonic individual-task curves and catastrophic degradation at sufficiently large decay. The more defensible claim is that a moderate, setting-dependent value often improves post-fine-tuning performance relative to the 0.1 default.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled weight-decay sweeps cover two architectures, model sizes up to 4B parameters, 20- and 140-token-per-parameter regimes, twelve downstream datasets, and additional pretraining/fine-tuning hyperparameter sweeps. Significance: The result that the weight decay minimizing pretraining loss can differ from that maximizing downstream performance is practically relevant and usefully questions validation loss as the sole criterion for selecting pretrained checkpoints.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized. Its main comparisons, training configurations, dataset sizes, and extensive per-task results are documented in the appendix, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges the restricted scale and correlational nature of the proposed mechanisms.

Originality: Studying pretraining weight decay specifically through downstream adaptability is a useful synthesis of plasticity and language-model optimization, even though several mechanistic observations build directly on prior work.
No major research-ethics concern is apparent: the study uses established datasets and includes a safety-alignment evaluation.
weaknesses: The central construct is not convincingly identified. Plasticity is defined as absolute held-out performance after fine-tuning, which conflates ability to learn from new data with pretrained knowledge, representation quality, initialization quality, and ordinary transfer performance. The paper does not report downstream performance before fine-tuning, improvement relative to that baseline, learning curves, training-set fit, or acquisition of genuinely novel knowledge. The claim that weight decay improves plasticity is therefore substantially stronger than the evidence-supported claim that it improves final fine-tuned performance.

There appear to be no independent pretraining or fine-tuning repetitions, random-seed analysis, confidence intervals, or statistical tests for the central results. Many reported differences are small, and averaging tasks or multiple metrics computed from the same generated samples does not quantify training variance. Consequently, the causal assertion that varying only weight decay establishes the effect is not adequately supported.

The causal comparison is further weakened because the weight-decay-0.1 checkpoints for Llama-2-4B-20x and OLMo-2-1B-140x are imported from separate prior projects while the other variants are newly trained. Without demonstrating identical code, data ordering, initialization, and execution conditions, weight decay is not necessarily the only differing factor in those groups.

The proposed mechanisms do not explain the downstream effect. Linear separability, attention pseudo-rank, parameter norm, overfitting, and downstream performance all co-vary with weight decay, but there are no mediation or intervention experiments. The overfitting analysis is limited to one OLMo-2-1B-20x setting and a very small train-validation-gap change without uncertainty; the low-rank result largely reproduces an existing theoretical and empirical finding. The manuscript acknowledges correlation but still repeatedly presents these observations as mechanistic explanations.

The practical recommendation that the optimal weight decay exceeds 0.1 is not portable as stated. Effective AdamW shrinkage depends on learning-rate magnitude and schedule, number of steps, batch size, and which parameter groups are decayed. The 20- and 140-TPP experiments even use different learning-rate schedules, yet no normalized decay measure or scaling rule is derived.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although many headline hyperparameters are provided, the manuscript supplies no usable code/model link in the reviewed PDF and omits seeds, initialization and data-order controls, exact decay parameter groups, full linear-probe training details, and sufficient procedural detail for several mechanistic measurements. Reproducing the many expensive pretraining runs would therefore be difficult.

The evidence is less diverse than the presentation suggests: four of the six CoT metrics are derived from the same sixteen samples, while MetaMathQA and SimpleScaling are both evaluated on the same GSM8KPlatinum-plus-MATH test collection. This makes the averages look broader than the number of independent evaluations warrants.

The impact statement is perfunctory and does not discuss the consequences of optimizing for adaptability, benchmark contamination, or limitations of reward-model-based safety evaluation. These are not fatal ethical issues, but the treatment is below the standard expected for a paper making safety-alignment claims. Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but construct validity, missing uncertainty, and incomplete controls require substantial revision before the central conclusion can be relied upon.

strengths: Soundness: The core intervention is clean—pretraining weight decay is varied while other settings are held fixed—and the main trend recurs across Llama-2 and OLMo-2, five model/training configurations, 20 and 140 tokens-per-parameter regimes, models up to 4B parameters, and twelve downstream tasks. The additional sweeps over pretraining learning rate and fine-tuning learning rate, weight decay, and batch size substantially strengthen the central empirical observation.

Significance: The finding that the weight decay minimizing pretraining validation loss can differ from the value maximizing post-fine-tuning performance is practically important. The OLMo-2-1B-140x example is especially informative: weight decay 0.1 gives lower pretraining loss, while 0.3 or 1.0 gives better downstream performance.

Originality: Connecting pretraining weight decay to later adaptability is a useful and relatively underexplored perspective. Although individual observations such as weight-decay-induced low-rank attention have precedent, the end-to-end study of pretraining selection, downstream adaptation, and stability–plasticity trade-offs forms a coherent contribution.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, clearly distinguishes optimization for pretraining loss from optimization for downstream performance, and provides extensive task-level plots and appendices. It also appropriately labels the proposed mechanisms as correlational and explicitly limits its conclusions to the examined scales, regimes, and forms of post-training.

Reproducibility: The manuscript reports architectures, token budgets, weight-decay grids, optimizer settings, schedules, fine-tuning hyperparameters, dataset sizes, prompts, decoding temperatures, and evaluation models. These details make the overall experimental pipeline comparatively transparent.

The representation, attention-rank, overfitting, upstream-retention, and hyperparameter-sweep analyses provide useful triangulation rather than relying on a single downstream score. No unresolved material ethical concern is apparent, and the safety-alignment experiment is relevant to the stated scope.
weaknesses: Soundness: The principal results do not report independent pretraining or fine-tuning repetitions, uncertainty intervals, or statistical tests. Most curves appear to represent a single run per configuration. Because optimization randomness and data order can affect both pretraining and fine-tuning, the claim that the effect is causal merely because only weight decay was intentionally changed is stronger than the evidence warrants. Repeated runs at representative weight-decay values are needed to establish the size and reliability of the effect.

The paper operationalizes plasticity almost entirely as final downstream performance after a fixed fine-tuning budget. This conflates adaptability with the quality and task relevance of the pretrained representation: a model may finish higher because it starts from more useful features, not because its parameters are intrinsically easier to update. Learning curves, early-step improvement, matched-initial-performance comparisons, or established plasticity diagnostics would better isolate the claimed construct.

The strongest phrasing is not uniformly supported task by task. Figure 8 contains non-monotonic and sometimes weak trends, especially for smaller models and metrics such as Pass@16; Figure 11 likewise shows dataset-specific exceptions. The aggregate trend is persuasive, but statements that higher weight decay 'consistently' improves performance should be qualified to exclude overly large values and acknowledge these exceptions.

The mechanistic account remains speculative. Linear-probe accuracy, attention pseudo-rank, and train–validation gap all co-vary with weight decay and downstream performance, but no mediation or intervention establishes that they cause improved adaptation. The overfitting evidence is particularly narrow, being shown only for OLMo-2-1B-20x, and the reported train–validation-gap changes are small.

The scale and post-training coverage limit significance: the largest model is 4B, only one configuration is trained at 140 TPP, and adaptation is restricted to supervised fine-tuning. It is therefore unclear whether the recommended values transfer to contemporary larger models or preference/RL-based post-training. The optimum is also selected from coarse grids—only three weight-decay settings for the 4B model and four for the 140-TPP model—so claims about an 'optimal' value should be softened.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive hyperparameter tables: random seeds, data-shuffling details, uncertainty computation, exact validation-set construction, linear-probe training and regularization details, reward-model evaluation implementation, and code/checkpoint version identifiers are not fully specified in the manuscript. Compute requirements are also substantial, which makes released checkpoints and scripts especially important.

The safety conclusion rests on only 100 harmful prompts and a single automated harmfulness evaluator. This is acceptable as a supplementary experiment but is too limited to support broad claims about safety-alignment plasticity. The impact statement is also boilerplate and could more directly discuss the dual-use implications of making models easier to adapt, including easier harmful fine-tuning.
